title.narrative: Strengthening Namibia’s Health, Financing and Community Systems, capacity, and resilience toward a sustained epidemic control of HIV/AIDS, TB, and Malaria - Namibia (01-Jan-2024-31-Dec-2026)

description.narrative: Namibia, Multicomponent, Ministry of Health and Social Services of Namibia (MOH)This program has the following goals: Reduce the number of people newly infected with HIV per year to less than 1 out of 1000 people (0.1% of the general population). Reduce the number of people dying of AIDS-related causes per year to less than 1 out of 1000 people (0.1% of the general population)-The number of people newly infected with HIV per year is less than the number of people dying of AIDS-related causes.. 62% reduction in TB incidence rate by 2027. 90% reduction in the number of TB deaths. Achievement of zero indigenous malaria cases in Namibia by 2027. Prevention of re-introduction and establishment of local malaria transmission in in eliminated and non-receptive areas. The objectives of this program are: To reduce new HIV infections by 75% by 2027. To reduce HIV related mortality rate from 1.06% in 2023 to 0.66% by 2027. To enroll and retain 100% of newly identified PLHIV on ART by 2023. To ensure 100% ART coverage among TB/HIV co-infected patients by 2023. To accelerate TB case detection and achieve universal drug susceptibility testing for TB by 2027. To manage all forms of TB, among all ages and including drug-resistant and drug-sensitive TB, and achieve a treatment success rate of 90% by 2027. To provide effective leadership and coordination for optimal implementation of malaria elimination interventions at all levels by 2025. Enhance and sustain the malaria elimination surveillance system for evidence-based decisions and actions in all districts by 2025. To protect 100% of the targeted population living in malaria areas with at least one appropriate vector control intervention by 2025. All suspected malaria cases are tested and 100% of confirmed malaria cases treated according to the national guidelines by 2025. By 2025, 100% of the population at risk utilize malaria interventions
